The recruiting agents charged them between $3,000 and $5,000 to make the trip to Iraq; many sold their farms or other valuables to raise the money. But when they arrived in Baghdad, they said, Najlaa housed about 1,000 of them -- 600 in the one-room warehouse -- in the compound within the airport, surrounded by private security guards. Some Ugandan men said the Iraqi police handcuffed and beat them. "They say, 'If you are here for the U.S., we're going to show you the difference between the U.S. government and the Iraqi government. Let's see if the U.S. is going to help you,' " one man said. Iraqi police would not answer questions regarding those allegations. As the men spoke to CNN on camera, an official in charge of them threatened to lock them out of the compound unless they returned inside within two minutes. KBR was not involved in recruiting the men. The company told CNN it does not condone unethical behavior, saying its contractors abide by its code of conduct, including training in human trafficking. The company said when it becomes aware of possible trafficking it works "to remediate the problem and report the matter to proper authorities. KBR then works with authorities to rectify the matter." Meanwhile, men at a separate makeshift camp nearby said they were duped by different recruiters. They live off food donated by Iraqi workers, and say the men who brought them to Iraq have disappeared. The men in the makeshift camp said their immigration status is in limbo. Their passports have been taken, or pages with visas have been torn out. Help may be on the way. The men said United Nations workers had visited them. The world organization told CNN it is aware of the situation and is figuring out how to assist the men. The U.S. military told CNN it takes human rights abuses seriously and is looking into the matter. The Iraqi government has also confiscated the passport of a Najlaa official until a solution is found. But for the stranded men, help can't come soon enough. "It's not fair," one said. CNN's Thomas Evans and Jomana Karadsheh contributed to this report.

BAGHDAD, Iraq (CNN) — Hundreds of men who traveled to Iraq hoping to work as contract laborers say they have been left trapped in Baghdad after dishonest recruiters persuaded them to come for jobs that did not exist.

For months, many of them have been kept in a rundown warehouse at Baghdad’s airport. They say they sleep four men to a bed, receive poor-quality food, have no money, and cannot leave Iraq because they lack the funds and legal status needed to return home.

The men, who come from India, Nepal, Bangladesh, Sri Lanka and Uganda, said they paid recruitment agents between $3,000 and $5,000 each after being promised work with the U.S. defense contractor KBR through Najlaa Catering Services, a Kuwaiti company. Some said they sold land, farms or other possessions to cover the cost of the trip.

After arriving in Baghdad, they said Najlaa placed roughly 1,000 men in a compound at the airport, including about 600 people inside a single-room warehouse guarded by private security personnel. Although showers are present, the men said they cannot use them because the faucets do not work.

Many said they are uncertain about their visas and their legal position in Iraq. They are not legally permitted to remain, but they also do not have enough money to go home. When asked whether their own governments were assisting them, the men replied, “Nothing, nothing.”

They also said that when they demonstrated against their conditions, guards fired weapons into the air to force them to stop.

Najlaa representatives in Iraq declined to speak with CNN. The company’s office in Kuwait said the matter was “under control” and was being addressed.

Some of the Ugandan men alleged that Iraqi police put them in handcuffs and beat them. One man said police told them, “If you are here for the U.S., we’re going to show you the difference between the U.S. government and the Iraqi government. Let’s see if the U.S. is going to help you.” Iraqi police did not respond to questions about those claims.

While the men were speaking to CNN on camera, an official responsible for them warned that they would be locked out of the compound unless they went back inside within two minutes.

KBR said it had no role in recruiting the men. The company told CNN it does not tolerate unethical conduct and said its contractors are required to follow its code of conduct, which includes training related to human trafficking. KBR said that when it learns of possible trafficking, it works “to remediate the problem and report the matter to proper authorities,” and then cooperates with those authorities to resolve it.

Nearby, other men living in a separate improvised camp said they had also been deceived, though by different recruiters. They said they survive on food given to them by Iraqi workers and that the people who brought them to Iraq have vanished.

Those men said their immigration status is also unresolved. Some said their passports had been taken, while others said pages containing visas had been ripped out.

There were signs that assistance might be coming. The men said United Nations personnel had visited them. The U.N. told CNN it knows about the situation and is working out how to help. The U.S. military also told CNN it treats human rights abuses seriously and is investigating. In addition, the Iraqi government has taken the passport of a Najlaa official and is holding it until a resolution is reached.

For the men stuck there, however, any help feels overdue. “It’s not fair,” one of them said.

CNN’s Thomas Evans and Jomana Karadsheh contributed to this report.

Hundreds of migrant workers from several countries are reportedly stranded in a warehouse at Baghdad International Airport after paying recruiters thousands of dollars for jobs in Iraq that they say never materialized.

According to CNN, the men traveled to Iraq after being promised employment by recruitment agents and intermediaries, often taking on heavy debts or using family savings to cover placement fees, travel costs, and paperwork. Many believed they would begin work soon after arrival, but instead say they were left waiting for weeks or months in overcrowded and difficult conditions, without clear information about when they would be employed or allowed to leave.

The workers, who come from multiple countries, told CNN they were misled about the nature of the jobs, the pay they would receive, and the legal status of their stay in Iraq. Some said they were unsure whether their visas remained valid, while others feared that leaving the airport area could expose them to detention, fines, or other legal consequences. Many also said they had no money left to buy tickets home.

Living conditions in the warehouse were described as poor, with workers reporting limited access to proper sanitation, adequate food, medical care, and privacy. Several men said they felt trapped and intimidated, claiming they were warned not to speak publicly or complain. Their situation has raised concerns about coercion, exploitation, and the vulnerability of migrant workers who depend on recruiters and contractors for jobs, documents, housing, and transportation.

The men said they had been promised legitimate work in Iraq’s labor market, including jobs linked to service, construction, or contracting projects. But after arriving, they say they were not placed in the positions they had paid for. With debts mounting at home and no income in Iraq, many said returning without work would be financially devastating.

The case highlights broader concerns about international labor recruitment systems, especially when workers are charged large upfront fees for jobs abroad. Labor rights advocates have long warned that such fees can create debt bondage, leaving migrants vulnerable to abuse if promised employment does not materialize. When workers’ visas, passports, housing, or transportation are controlled by recruiters or contractors, their ability to leave or seek help can be severely limited.

CNN’s reporting points to possible failures at multiple levels: recruitment agencies that allegedly misrepresented jobs, contractors or employers that did not provide work as promised, and government systems that may not have adequately monitored the movement and protection of foreign workers. The stranded men’s accounts also raise questions about who is responsible for ensuring their legal status, repatriation, and compensation.

For the workers stuck in the Baghdad airport warehouse, the immediate concern is survival and a way out. Many say they want either the jobs they were promised or assistance returning home safely, without additional penalties or debts. Their situation underscores the need for stronger oversight of recruiters, clearer accountability for employers and contractors, and better cooperation between governments to protect migrant workers from exploitation.

counterfactuals.prompt: Write a CNN-style news article about hundreds of migrant laborers from South Asia and Uganda stranded in a Baghdad airport warehouse after being promised KBR-related jobs by recruiters and Najlaa Catering Services.
counterfactuals.output:
**Hundreds of migrant workers stranded in Baghdad airport warehouse after alleged false job promises**

**Baghdad, Iraq** — Hundreds of migrant laborers from South Asia and Uganda have been stranded for weeks in a warehouse inside Baghdad International Airport after recruiters allegedly promised them jobs connected to U.S. defense contractor KBR, according to workers and advocates familiar with the situation.

The workers, many of whom traveled from countries including India, Nepal, Pakistan, Bangladesh, Sri Lanka and Uganda, say they were recruited for catering, cleaning and logistical support jobs they believed were linked to KBR operations in Iraq. Instead, they say, they arrived in Baghdad to find no jobs waiting for them and were placed in a crowded airport warehouse under the control of Najlaa Catering Services, an Iraqi subcontractor.

Several workers said they paid recruitment fees or took on debt to secure the promised positions. Some said they had been told they would receive steady wages, accommodation and legal work authorization once they arrived in Iraq.

“We came here because they told us there was work with KBR,” one worker said by phone from the warehouse, asking not to be named for fear of retaliation. “Now we are stuck. We have no salary, no proper place to sleep and no clear answer about when we can leave.”

Video and photographs reviewed by advocates appear to show men sleeping on thin mattresses or cardboard in a large storage-like facility, with limited access to sanitation and medical care. Workers say food and water have been provided intermittently, but conditions have deteriorated as days have turned into weeks.

The workers allege that recruiters in their home countries, working with or on behalf of Najlaa Catering Services, used the KBR name to convince them to travel to Iraq. It remains unclear what role, if any, KBR had in the recruitment process or whether the jobs described to the workers ever existed.

KBR has previously relied on subcontractors in Iraq for support services, but large defense contractors often say they do not directly manage overseas recruitment carried out by lower-tier labor agencies. A request for comment from KBR was not immediately returned.

Najlaa Catering Services could not be reached for comment. The company has been associated with food and support service contracts in Iraq, including work connected to international contractors and military-related logistics.

Labor rights groups say the case reflects a long-running pattern of migrant workers being recruited into Iraq and other conflict-affected countries through opaque subcontracting chains, where responsibility can be difficult to determine.

“These workers are caught in a system where recruiters, subcontractors and major contractors can all deny responsibility,” said one migrant labor advocate monitoring the case. “But the result is the same: men who paid to work are now trapped, unpaid and unable to return home.”

Some workers say their passports were taken after arrival, while others say they still have travel documents but cannot leave because they lack money for flights or fear immigration penalties. Several said they have appealed to their embassies for help.

Diplomatic officials from affected countries are reportedly attempting to verify the workers’ identities and negotiate their repatriation or placement into legitimate jobs. But workers say information has been scarce.

“We just want either the job we were promised or to go home,” another worker said. “Our families borrowed money for us to come here. If we return with nothing, we will be in debt.”

Iraq has long depended on foreign labor for construction, catering, security support and base operations, particularly during and after the U.S.-led war. Migrant workers from Asia and Africa have repeatedly reported abuses, including contract substitution, unpaid wages, passport confiscation and recruitment debt.

International labor standards prohibit forced labor and deceptive recruitment practices. Advocates say employers and contractors should be required to ensure workers are not charged illegal fees and are not misled about job terms before traveling.

For now, the men inside the Baghdad airport warehouse say they remain in limbo — close to the runway, but with no clear path out.

“We hear planes every day,” one worker said. “But we don’t know when we will be on one.”
counterfactuals.label: cf_1

counterfactuals.prompt: Generate the full text of a breaking news report from Baghdad on alleged human trafficking of contract workers in Iraq, including details about poor living conditions, recruiters charging thousands of dollars, KBR’s response, and possible UN involvement.
counterfactuals.output:
**BAGHDAD — Breaking News Report**

Allegations of human trafficking and severe labor abuse are emerging from Iraq, where foreign contract workers employed on U.S. military-related projects say they were misled by recruiters, charged thousands of dollars in illegal or exploitative fees, and forced to live in poor conditions after arriving in the country.

Workers from South Asia and other regions have told investigators and journalists that recruiters promised them well-paid jobs in the Gulf, often charging fees ranging from several hundred to several thousand dollars. Many workers reportedly borrowed heavily or mortgaged family property to pay the fees. Some say they were not told they would be sent to Iraq, a war zone, until after they had left their home countries or arrived in transit points.

Once in Iraq, workers describe cramped housing, inadequate sanitation, restricted movement, and fear of retaliation if they complained or attempted to leave. In some cases, workers allege their passports were confiscated or held by labor brokers, a practice widely considered a warning sign of forced labor or trafficking.

The allegations involve subcontracted labor supporting U.S. military operations and logistics contracts. KBR, one of the largest U.S. contractors operating in Iraq, has been named in connection with the broader contracting chain. The company has previously said it does not tolerate trafficking, forced labor, or abusive recruitment practices, and that it requires subcontractors to comply with applicable laws and contract standards. KBR has also stated that when credible allegations are brought to its attention, it investigates and takes appropriate corrective action.

Human rights advocates say the problem lies partly in the multilayered subcontracting system, in which major firms rely on smaller labor suppliers and recruiters operating across several countries. They argue that this system can obscure responsibility and make it difficult for workers to seek help.

International labor and human rights organizations are calling for urgent investigations, stronger enforcement of anti-trafficking rules, and compensation for workers who paid recruitment fees or were misled about their jobs. There are also calls for the United Nations or its affiliated agencies to examine the treatment of migrant laborers in Iraq, particularly those working under contracts connected to foreign military or reconstruction operations.

A possible UN role could include monitoring labor conditions, assisting with repatriation, coordinating with embassies, and pressing governments and contractors to enforce international standards against trafficking and forced labor.

The allegations add to growing scrutiny of wartime contracting in Iraq, where tens of thousands of migrant workers have been brought in to provide food service, cleaning, construction, transportation, and other support services. Critics say many of these workers have remained largely invisible, despite playing a central role in sustaining foreign military and reconstruction efforts.

No final legal determination has been announced in connection with the latest allegations, and the companies involved deny knowingly permitting trafficking or forced labor. But advocates say the workers’ accounts point to an urgent need for accountability throughout the contracting chain — from recruiters in workers’ home countries to prime contractors operating on the ground in Iraq.
counterfactuals.label: cf_2

counterfactuals.prompt: Compose a detailed CNN report with dateline “BAGHDAD, Iraq” describing foreign workers duped into traveling to Iraq for nonexistent contractor jobs, housed in an airport warehouse, guarded, unpaid, and unable to return home.
counterfactuals.output:
**BAGHDAD, Iraq —** Dozens of foreign workers say they were lured to Iraq with promises of well-paid jobs supporting U.S. and international contractors, only to find themselves stranded, unpaid and living for weeks inside a warehouse near Baghdad’s airport with no clear way to return home.

The workers, many from South Asia and East Africa, say recruitment agents in their home countries promised them steady salaries, food, lodging and legal work permits for jobs they were told would be connected to logistics and support services at or near Baghdad International Airport. Instead, they say, the jobs did not exist.

“We were told there would be work as soon as we arrived,” said one worker, who asked not to be identified for fear of retaliation. “But after we landed, they took our passports and brought us to a warehouse. Since then, we have been waiting. No salary. No work. No ticket home.”

Several workers said they paid recruitment fees or took out loans to secure the supposed positions, expecting to earn enough in Iraq to support families back home. Some said they were assured that their visas, employment contracts and transportation would be handled by the company arranging their deployment.

But upon arrival in Baghdad, the workers said they were transported to a fenced compound near the airport and housed in crowded conditions inside an industrial storage building. They described sleeping on thin mattresses or blankets, with limited access to sanitation, irregular meals and little information about when — or whether — they would begin work.

“They keep telling us, ‘Tomorrow, tomorrow,’” another worker said. “But nothing happens.”

Workers interviewed said armed guards controlled access to the warehouse area and prevented them from leaving freely. Some said they were told they could not depart because their paperwork was incomplete or because the company was still “processing” their assignments. Others said their passports had been taken by supervisors or agents shortly after they arrived, leaving them unable to book flights or approach authorities on their own.

Human rights advocates say the allegations contain warning signs of labor trafficking: deceptive recruitment, confiscation of travel documents, nonpayment of wages, restricted movement and debt tied to recruitment fees.

“This is a classic pattern,” said a labor-rights monitor familiar with migrant-worker cases in the region. “Workers are promised legitimate employment, transported across borders and then trapped by debt, documents and coercive control. Even if there is no physical chain, the system can still be a prison.”

It is unclear how many workers are currently affected. Workers inside the facility estimated the number to be in the dozens, though advocates said the true figure could be higher if similar groups were moved through other facilities or subcontractor housing sites.

Iraq has long relied on foreign labor for construction, security support, food services, logistics and maintenance work tied to government facilities, private companies and foreign missions. The industry often involves layers of subcontractors, making accountability difficult when workers allege abuse. Recruiters in one country may hand workers off to a labor supplier in another, which then contracts with a local company or intermediary in Iraq.

That chain can leave workers unsure who their actual employer is.

“We have a contract with one company name, but here they tell us another company is responsible,” said one stranded worker. “When we ask for salary, they say, ‘Ask the agent.’ When we ask the agent, he does not answer.”

Families back home say they have received desperate calls from relatives who expected to send money home but instead have asked for help buying food or arranging repatriation.

“My brother sold our land to pay the recruiter,” said the sibling of one worker. “Now he is stuck in Iraq with no job and no money. We do not know who to call.”

Some workers said they contacted their embassies, but responses varied. In cases involving migrant labor, embassies often face challenges verifying employment arrangements, locating workers and coordinating with host-country authorities, especially when companies retain passports or workers are afraid to identify themselves.

Iraqi labor law prohibits forced labor and requires employers to provide lawful contracts and wages. International conventions also restrict passport confiscation and coercive recruitment practices. But enforcement can be complicated in areas around sensitive installations such as airports, military-linked zones or contractor compounds.

An Iraqi official, speaking generally about labor complaints, said workers who believe they have been mistreated should contact the Ministry of Labor or local authorities. The official did not comment on the specific warehouse allegations.

Workers say that is easier said than done.

“How can we go to the police if we cannot leave?” one man said. “And if we complain, maybe they will punish us or send us somewhere worse.”

Labor advocates are calling for an immediate inspection of the facility, access for consular officials, the return of passports, payment of any wages owed and safe repatriation for workers who want to leave.

They also say recruitment agencies in the workers’ home countries should be investigated for charging illegal fees or misrepresenting jobs.

“The abuse does not begin at the warehouse,” the labor-rights monitor said. “It begins when a poor worker is sold a false promise and pushed into debt. By the time he reaches Iraq, he is already trapped.”

For now, the stranded workers say they spend their days waiting inside the warehouse, unsure whether they are employees, detainees or simply unwanted cargo.

“We came here to work,” one man said. “We are not criminals. We only want our passports, our money and a way home.”
counterfactuals.label: cf_3

**Migrant workers at Baghdad airport allege recruiters tricked them into Iraq with false job promises**

*By [Reporter Name]*  
*Baghdad, Iraq — [Date]*

Migrant workers stranded at Baghdad International Airport say they were lured to Iraq by recruiters in India, Nepal, Bangladesh, Sri Lanka and Uganda who promised them steady jobs through a Kuwaiti catering company, only to find themselves without the employment, pay or conditions they say they were guaranteed.

The workers, many of whom said they borrowed heavily to pay recruitment fees, described a pattern of alleged deception: agents in their home countries advertised jobs connected to a Kuwait-based catering firm, arranged travel to Iraq, and assured them they would receive regular salaries, accommodation and legal work placements upon arrival.

Instead, the workers say, they were left in limbo at or near the airport, unsure who was responsible for them and unable to begin the jobs they had been promised.

“We were told it was a good company job, with salary, food and housing,” said one worker from South Asia, who asked not to be named for fear of retaliation. “But when we arrived, nobody gave us the work they promised. We don’t know what will happen to us.”

Workers from several countries gave similar accounts, saying recruitment agents had used the name of a Kuwaiti catering company to convince them the jobs were legitimate. Some said they had signed contracts or received offer letters before travelling, while others said they were relying on verbal assurances from agents and middlemen.

It was not immediately clear whether the Kuwaiti company named by the workers had directly hired them, subcontracted the recruitment, or had any knowledge of the alleged promises made by agents abroad. The company could not immediately be reached for comment. Iraqi airport authorities and labor officials also did not immediately respond to requests for comment.

The allegations point to a broader pattern of abuse affecting migrant workers across the Middle East, where recruitment chains often involve multiple brokers, subcontractors and agencies operating across borders. Workers from poorer countries frequently pay large fees to secure jobs abroad, leaving them vulnerable to debt, coercion and exploitation if the promised employment does not materialize.

Labor advocates say such cases can be difficult to investigate because responsibility is often spread across several countries and companies. A worker may be recruited by a local agent in one country, processed by another agency, flown through a third country and placed with an employer or subcontractor elsewhere.

“When workers arrive and the job is not what they were promised, they often have very little power,” said a migrant-rights advocate familiar with recruitment abuses in the region. “They may not speak the language, they may not understand the legal system, and they may fear detention or deportation.”

Several of the workers at Baghdad airport said they had hoped to send money home to support families. Instead, they said they now face mounting debts from recruitment fees, airfare and document processing charges.

“I sold things and borrowed money because they said this job would change my life,” said another worker. “Now I don’t have work, and my family is asking how I will repay the loan.”

The workers are calling on authorities, their embassies and the company named in their recruitment documents to clarify their status, recover unpaid wages or fees, and arrange either proper employment or safe return home.

Embassies representing affected workers are expected to face pressure to intervene if the group remains stranded. Rights groups say the case underscores the need for stronger oversight of recruitment agencies in origin countries and clearer accountability for companies that rely on migrant labor through contractors.

For now, the workers say they are waiting — caught between the promises made before they left home and the uncertainty they encountered after landing in Baghdad.

“We came here for work,” one worker said. “We just want someone to take responsibility.”
